title: OOP II: Pythonic classes
subtitle: Objects that print, compare, sort and validate
goal: Make classes behave like built-in types with dunder methods, properties, class attributes, class methods and static methods.
outcomes: Choose between class attributes and instance attributes
Write __str__ and __repr__ for users and developers
Make objects comparable and sortable with __eq__ and __lt__, and sized with __len__

slides.title: Mission 25: Pythonic classes
slides.body:
Yesterday's objects work, but they feel clumsy: `print(acct)` shows a memory address, `==` says two identical objects differ, and `sorted()` refuses them.

Today your classes learn to behave like built-ins: print nicely, compare, sort, report their `len`, and validate their own data.

visual.verdict: Objects that explain themselves are easier to debug and use.

slides.say: Yesterday's objects work, but they feel clumsy. Printing one shows a cryptic memory address, two objects with identical data are not equal, and sorted refuses to sort them. Today your classes learn to behave like Python's own types. They will print nicely, compare and sort, report their length, and validate their own data.

slides.title: Class attributes: shared by all
slides.body:
An attribute set **in the class body** belongs to the class and is shared by every instance, like an interest rate. Attributes set on `self` belong to one object.

When you read `a.interest_rate`, Python looks on the object first, then on its class.
slides.say: So far every attribute was set on self, so each object had its own copy. An attribute written directly in the class body is different: it belongs to the class and is shared by every instance, like a bank's interest rate. When you read an attribute, Python looks on the object first, and if it is not there, it looks on the class.

slides.title: Shared settings with class attributes
slides.code:
class SavingsAccount:
    interest_rate = 0.04  # class attribute: shared by all accounts
    accounts_opened = 0

    def __init__(self, owner, balance):
        self.owner = owner  # instance attributes: one per object
        self.balance = balance
        SavingsAccount.accounts_opened += 1

    def yearly_interest(self):
        return self.balance * self.interest_rate


a = SavingsAccount("Riya", 10000)
b = SavingsAccount("Arjun", 50000)
print(a.yearly_interest(), b.yearly_interest())
print("Accounts opened:", SavingsAccount.accounts_opened)

SavingsAccount.interest_rate = 0.05  # the bank changes its rate
print(a.yearly_interest(), b.yearly_interest())
explain: Defined in the class body, so every account shares it.
Update the class attribute through the class name: a counter for all accounts.
self.interest_rate is not on the object, so Python finds it on the class.
Change it once on the class, and every account sees the new rate.
slides.say: The interest rate and the accounts opened counter live on the class, so they are shared. Owner and balance live on each object. Inside yearly interest, self dot interest rate is not found on the object, so Python looks it up on the class. When the bank changes its rate once, on the class, every account immediately sees the new value.

slides.title: Predict the output
slides.code:
class Team:
    players = 11


a = Team()
b = Team()
a.players = 12
print(a.players, b.players, Team.players)
slides.why: Assigning `a.players = 12` creates a **new instance attribute** on `a` that hides the class one. `b` and `Team` still see 11. To change the shared value, assign through the class: `Team.players = 12`.
slides.say: The class says a team has eleven players. Then we assign twelve through the object a. What do a, b and the class each see? This trips up experienced developers too.

slides.title: __str__ and __repr__
slides.body:
Two methods control how an object turns into text:

- `__str__`: friendly text for **users**, used by `print()` and f-strings
- `__repr__`: precise text for **developers**, used in lists, the shell and debuggers. Ideally it looks like code that would recreate the object.

If you write only one, write `__repr__`: `print` falls back to it.
slides.say: Two special methods control how your object turns into text. Dunder str is the friendly version for users, used by print and f strings. Dunder repr is the precise version for developers, shown inside lists, in the Python shell and in debuggers, and ideally it looks like the code that would recreate the object. If you only write one, write repr, because print falls back to it.

slides.title: A Book that explains itself
slides.code:
class Book:
    def __init__(self, title, author, price):
        self.title = title
        self.author = author
        self.price = price

    def __str__(self):
        return f"{self.title} by {self.author}, ₹{self.price}"

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Book({self.title!r}, {self.author!r}, {self.price})"


b = Book("Wings of Fire", "A. P. J. Abdul Kalam", 399)
print(b)
print(f"Now reading: {b}")
print(repr(b))
print([b])
slides.expect:
Wings of Fire by A. P. J. Abdul Kalam, ₹399
Now reading: Wings of Fire by A. P. J. Abdul Kalam, ₹399
Book('Wings of Fire', 'A. P. J. Abdul Kalam', 399)
[Book('Wings of Fire', 'A. P. J. Abdul Kalam', 399)]
explain: __str__ must return a string: the friendly version.
The !r inside the braces uses repr, so the strings appear with quotes, like real code.
print uses __str__.
So do f-strings.
A list shows its items with __repr__.
slides.say: Our book returns a friendly sentence from dunder str, and a code-like description from dunder repr. The exclamation r inside the f string braces means use repr, so the title appears with its quotes. Print and f strings use the friendly version. But a list shows each item with repr, which is why repr matters so much when you are debugging.

slides.title: Quick check
slides.q: A class defines **only** `__repr__`, not `__str__`. What does `print(obj)` show?
options: The memory address, like <Obj object at 0x...>
slides.why: When `__str__` is missing, Python falls back to `__repr__`. That is why a good `__repr__` is the first dunder method most developers write.
slides.say: Quick check. Your class defines dunder repr but not dunder str. What does print show?

slides.title: Dunder methods are hooks
slides.body: "Dunder" means **d**ouble **under**score. You never call these directly; Python calls them when you use normal syntax. Define the hook, and your object joins in.
slides.say: Dunder is short for double underscore. These special methods are hooks. You rarely call them yourself. Instead, Python calls them for you when you use normal syntax. Write len of x, and Python calls x dot dunder len. Write a less than b, and Python calls a dot dunder lt with b. Define the hook, and your object joins in with the rest of the language.

slides.title: Predict the output
options: TypeError: Point objects cannot be compared
slides.why: Without `__eq__`, `==` falls back to **identity**: are these the very same object? They are two separate objects, so the answer is False, even though their data matches.
slides.say: Two points with exactly the same coordinates. The class has no dunder methods yet. Are they equal? Predict, then run.

slides.title: __eq__ and __lt__: sortable versions
slides.body: Sorting software versions as **strings** is a real bug: `"3.9"` looks bigger than `"3.12"`. Compare them as tuples of numbers instead.
slides.expect:
True
False
True
[Version('3.9.0'), Version('3.10.4'), Version('3.12.1'), Version('3.13.0')]
Latest: Version('3.13.0')
explain: "3.12.1" becomes the tuple (3, 12, 1).
__eq__ decides what == means for versions.
__lt__ decides what < means; sorted only needs this one.
Strings compare character by character, and 9 beats 1: wrong answer.
Tuples of ints compare number by number: 9 is less than 12.
sorted and max now work on our own objects.
slides.say: Sorting version numbers as strings is a real bug that has shipped in real products, because the text three point nine looks bigger than three point twelve. Our Version class stores the numbers as a tuple. Dunder eq defines equality and dunder lt defines less than, by comparing those tuples. Now sorted and max just work, and they give the right answer.

slides.title: __len__: a playlist that knows its size
slides.expect:
2
Road trip (2 songs)
Focus is empty
explain: __len__ lets len() work on a Playlist.
Methods can use len(self) like any other code.
len(trip) calls trip.__len__().
With __len__ defined, an object of length 0 counts as False, just like an empty list.
slides.say: Give a class dunder len, and the built-in len works on it. Our playlist reports how many songs it holds, and its str method uses len of self too. Here is a bonus: once an object has a length, a length of zero counts as false, exactly like an empty list. So if not empty reads beautifully.

slides.title: @property: attributes with rules
slides.body:
A plain attribute can be set to anything: `s.marks = 140`. A **property** looks like an attribute from outside, but runs your code on every read or write, so it can **validate**.

The value itself is stored in `_marks`, with an underscore. The `@` line is a **decorator**; you will write your own on Day 29.

right.title: Property with a setter
right.code:
s.marks = 140
# ValueError: marks must be
# between 0 and 100

visual.verdict: Same syntax for the caller, but the class enforces its rules.

slides.say: A plain attribute accepts anything, so nothing stops marks from being set to a hundred and forty. A property looks exactly like an attribute from the outside, but it runs your code every time someone reads or writes it, so it can validate. The real value is kept in an attribute with a leading underscore. The at sign line is called a decorator, and on day twenty nine you will write your own.

slides.title: Validated marks
slides.expect:
Meera 72
Rejected: marks must be between 0 and 100, got 140
Still 72
explain: Even __init__ goes through the setter, so bad data is rejected from the start.
@property: reading s.marks runs this method.
@marks.setter: writing s.marks = value runs this one.
The real value lives in _marks.
Looks like a plain assignment, but the setter checks it.
The bad value never got in.
slides.say: The property called marks has a getter, which returns the stored value, and a setter, which checks the range before storing it in underscore marks. Even dunder init goes through the setter, so a student can never be created with bad marks. From outside it looks like a plain attribute, but a hundred and forty is rejected and the old value stays.

slides.title: Predict the output
slides.why: A property is **computed on every read**, so it always reflects the current radius: 3.14 × 10² = 314.0. That is the advantage over storing area once in `__init__`, where it would go stale.
slides.say: The circle's area is a property. We create a circle of radius two, then change the radius to ten, then read the area. Which area do we get?

slides.title: @classmethod and @staticmethod
slides.body:
Two more kinds of method:

- `@classmethod` receives the **class** as `cls`. Perfect for alternative constructors ("factories") like `User.from_csv(line)`.
- `@staticmethod` receives nothing automatic. It is a plain helper function that lives in the class because it belongs there.
slides.say: Two more kinds of method. A class method receives the class itself, called cls, instead of an object. It is perfect for alternative constructors, often called factories, like building a user from a line of CSV. A static method receives nothing automatically. It is just a helper function that lives inside the class because that is where it logically belongs.

slides.title: Factories and helpers
slides.body: Users arrive from a CSV import, a JSON API and a signup form. Factories give each source its own clean constructor.
explain: A class method: called on the class, receives it as cls.
cls(...) builds a new object, the same as User(...).
A second factory, for data that came from JSON.
A static method: no self, no cls, just a related helper.
Call factories on the class itself.
slides.say: Real apps receive users from many places: a CSV import, a JSON API, a signup form. Class methods give each source its own clean constructor. From csv splits the line and calls cls, which builds a new user. From dict does the same for JSON data. And is valid email is a static method, a helper that belongs with users but needs no particular user to run.

slides.title: Pick the right tool
slides.q: You want `Order.from_json(text)` to parse JSON and return a new `Order`. What should `from_json` be?
slides.why: An alternative constructor has no object yet, so it cannot take `self`. A `@classmethod` gets the class as `cls` and returns `cls(...)`, which also works for subclasses (Day 26).
slides.say: You want a method that parses JSON text and returns a brand new order. There is no order object yet when you call it. Which kind of method should it be?

slides.title: Fix the bug
slides.task:
Printing a `Ticket` crashes with **TypeError: __str__ returned non-string**. Fix `__str__` so `print(t)` shows:

`PNR 4521367890: Rajdhani Express, seat B2-34`
slides.tests:
t2 = Ticket("8102233445", "Vande Bharat", "C4-12")
assert str(t2) == "PNR 8102233445: Vande Bharat, seat C4-12", f"str() should give 'PNR 8102233445: Vande Bharat, seat C4-12', got {str(t2)!r}."
assert "PNR 4521367890: Rajdhani Express, seat B2-34" in __out__, "print(t) should show the ticket line."
assert __out__.count("PNR") == 1, "__str__ should return the text, not print it. Only the print(t) call should print."
hints: __str__ must give its text back to Python, not show it.
slides.say: Printing this train ticket crashes with a type error saying dunder str returned a non string. Remember the difference between return and print from day seventeen. Dunder str must hand its text back to Python.

slides.title: A sortable leaderboard
slides.task:
Make `Player` objects work on a leaderboard:

- `__repr__` returns `Player('Riya', 120)`
- `__eq__`: equal when name **and** score match
- `__lt__`: compares by score, so `sorted(players)` goes from lowest to highest
slides.tests:
p = Player("Riya", 120)
assert repr(p) == "Player('Riya', 120)", f"repr should look like Player('Riya', 120), got {repr(p)}."
assert Player("Riya", 120) == Player("Riya", 120), "Two players with the same name and score should be equal. Define __eq__."
assert Player("Riya", 120) != Player("Riya", 99), "Same name but a different score should not be equal."
assert Player("Kabir", 95) < Player("Riya", 120), "Kabir (95) should be less than Riya (120). Define __lt__ by score."
ranked = sorted([Player("Riya", 120), Player("Kabir", 95), Player("Meera", 140)])
assert [x.name for x in ranked] == ["Kabir", "Riya", "Meera"], f"sorted should order by score: Kabir, Riya, Meera. Got {ranked}."
assert max(ranked).name == "Meera", "max should find the top scorer."
hints: __repr__ can use an f-string with !r for the name: f"Player({self.name!r}, {self.score})"
__eq__ returns self.name == other.name and self.score == other.score
slides.say: Let's make a leaderboard. Give the player class a developer friendly repr, an equality method that compares both name and score, and a less than method that compares scores. Then sorted and max will work on players out of the box.

slides.title: A validated sensor reading
slides.task:
An IoT sensor reports temperatures. Write `Reading`:

- a `celsius` **property** whose setter raises `ValueError` below -273.15 (absolute zero)
- a read-only `fahrenheit` property: `celsius * 9 / 5 + 32`
- a `@classmethod` `from_fahrenheit(cls, f)` that returns a new `Reading`
slides.tests:
r = Reading(30)
assert r.celsius == 30 and r.fahrenheit == 86.0, "Reading(30) should have celsius 30 and fahrenheit 86.0."
r.celsius = 100
assert r.fahrenheit == 212.0, "fahrenheit should be calculated from the current celsius: 100 C is 212 F."
for bad in (-300, -273.16):
    try:
        Reading(bad)
        raise AssertionError(f"Reading({bad}) is below absolute zero and should raise ValueError. Validate in the celsius setter.")
    except ValueError:
        pass
assert Reading(-273.15).celsius == -273.15, "Exactly -273.15 is allowed."
try:
    r.celsius = -500
except ValueError:
    pass
assert r.celsius == 100, "A rejected value must not replace the old one."
f = Reading.from_fahrenheit(212)
assert isinstance(f, Reading) and round(f.celsius, 2) == 100, "from_fahrenheit(212) should return a Reading of 100 C."
assert isinstance(Reading.__dict__.get("fahrenheit"), property), "fahrenheit should be a @property."
hints: Copy the pattern from the Student example: @property for celsius, then @celsius.setter that validates and stores in self._celsius.
fahrenheit is a @property with no setter.
from_fahrenheit converts with (f - 32) * 5 / 9 and returns cls(that).
slides.say: A temperature sensor in a smart home reports readings. Make celsius a validated property that refuses anything below absolute zero, minus two seventy three point one five. Add fahrenheit as a read only property, and a class method that builds a reading from fahrenheit.

slides.title: Mission 25 complete
points: Class attributes are shared; instance attributes belong to one object
Dunder methods are hooks: __eq__ for ==, __lt__ for sorting, __len__ for len()
@property validates on write and computes on read, with plain attribute syntax
slides.say: Mission twenty five complete. Your classes now print themselves clearly, compare and sort, know their length, and guard their own data with properties. Tomorrow we build families of classes with inheritance, and learn when to use composition instead. See you on day twenty six.
